_doc: Per-cuisine intro paragraphs (1-2 sentences), 3 related cuisines, and optional community_partners. Used by inject_openings.py to differentiate /cuisine/* SEO landing pages. Toronto-specific where possible; avoid templated phrasing. Edit freely; the next cron run picks up changes. Schema: {intro: str, related: [key, key, key], community_partners?: [{name, url, blurb}]}. community_partners renders as a quiet footer block of reciprocal outbound links to cultural-community directories that list our cuisine page back; add an entry only AFTER a directory confirms they'll list you (otherwise you're sending traffic out for nothing). Cap of 4 per cuisine enforced in the renderer.

afghan.intro: Afghan kabob houses cluster along the GTA's western edge - Etobicoke, Mississauga, the Queensway - where the diaspora settled in waves from the 1980s on. Look for chapli kabob, mantu dumplings, and long basmati pilafs studded with raisins and carrots.

african_west.intro: Catch-all for places drawing on multiple West African traditions - Nigerian, Ghanaian, Senegalese - that share a kitchen rather than committing to one. The country-specific pages cover the more focused spots.

argentinian.intro: Steak and chimichurri lead, but a strong empanada subculture has grown across the west end and Bloor West. Toronto's Argentinian rooms tend to be small and family-run rather than the big asado halls you'd find in Buenos Aires.

armenian.intro: Armenian kitchens here often overlap with Persian and Lebanese influences - lahmajun, manti, dolma - reflecting the diaspora's long path through the Levant before landing in Canada. The community concentrates in North York and Thornhill.

bangladeshi.intro: Distinct from Indian and Pakistani despite frequent confusion: Bangladeshi menus lean on fish (especially hilsa), mustard-oil pungency, and a different spice profile. The community sits heaviest along Scarborough's Danforth-Victoria Park stretch.

brazilian.intro: Coxinhas, picanha, and pão de queijo show up across a small but growing scene, mostly bakery-cafés and churrascarias rather than regional Bahian or Nordeste cooking. Anchored downtown and in Mississauga.

caribbean.intro: Multi-island spots that don't commit to one country - or places where the menu spans Jamaican, Trinidadian, and Guyanese without favouring one. The country-specific pages cover the more focused kitchens.

chinese.intro: Several distinct scenes: old Chinatown on Spadina (Cantonese, Toishanese), the Markham-Scarborough corridor (Hong Kong + northern), and a newer wave of mainland regional cooking - Sichuan, Hunan, Yunnan - opening downtown and at Yonge & Finch.

colombian.intro: Bandeja paisa, arepas, and slow-cooked sancocho across a community settled mostly in the west end. The round, griddle-cooked Colombian arepa is a different animal from the flatter Venezuelan one - both surface on the same blocks.

dominican.intro: Mangú, sancocho, and small bachata-cooking rooms that have started appearing across North York. A younger scene compared to most other Latin cuisines in Toronto - most spots are first-generation immigrant-owned.

eritrean.intro: Often paired with Ethiopian on the same menu, but the cuisines diverge: more raw beef (kitfo), more zigni-style stews, and an Italian inheritance that surfaces as pasta dishes. The community overlaps with the Ethiopian one along Bloor West.

ethiopian.intro: Injera-and-stew kitchens have anchored the Bloor-Ossington intersection since the 1980s. Newer openings push east along the Danforth and into Scarborough, with a growing number leaning explicitly vegetarian (kik alicha, gomen, atakilt wat).

filipino.intro: Adobo, sinigang, lechon kawali. The community is large but the restaurant scene is younger than the population - most openings are recent, often kakanin (rice-cake) counters or small lunch spots in North York and Mississauga.

french.intro: From classical brasseries downtown to neighbourhood bistros along Queen West and Ossington. Recent openings have leaned Lyonnais and bouchon rather than the Paris-by-default model that dominated the 2000s.

ghanaian.intro: Jollof rice (the perennial Ghana-Nigeria debate continues), banku with tilapia, waakye. A small scene anchored along Jane and Finch and pushing west along Eglinton.

greek.intro: The Danforth's Greektown is the historical anchor - souvlaki houses going back to the 1960s - but new openings have spread to Etobicoke and the Junction, often leaning more Cretan or Aegean than the standard pita-grill template.

guyanese.intro: Pepperpot, roti, chow mein flavoured with cumin and pepper. Guyanese cooking is its own thing despite the broader Caribbean grouping - look for the Indo-Caribbean influences that distinguish it from Jamaican. Concentrated in Scarborough and the eastern 401 corridor.

indian.intro: The most-represented cuisine on the site by a wide margin. Gerrard India Bazaar is the historic anchor; newer regional kitchens (Hyderabadi, Chettinad, Goan, Bengali) keep splintering into their own buckets - we tag those separately when the menu commits to a region.

indonesian.intro: A small scene - rendang, gado-gado, nasi goreng - but a few recent openings have brought serious Padang and Javanese cooking to the city. Most spots cluster downtown.

italian.intro: Two Italies in Toronto: the postwar Calabrian and Sicilian one along Corso Italia and College, and a younger Roman/Bolognese wave downtown. New openings lean toward the second - single-dish pastificios, focaccerias, gelaterias.

jamaican.intro: Patties, jerk, ackee and saltfish. Eglinton West (Little Jamaica) is the cultural spine; Scarborough and the western 401 are where most new takeout counters open. Goat curry is a useful gauge of seriousness.

japanese.intro: Sushi led the wave in the 90s; now ramen, izakaya, and small-counter omakase rooms dominate new openings. Chef-owned single-counter ramen shops are pushing past the chain-ramen model that used to define the city.

jewish_deli.intro: Smoked meat, knishes, latkes, matzo ball soup. Toronto's deli scene is smaller than Montreal's but a few long-running rooms anchor it, and a recent revival-style wave has opened across the west end.

korean.intro: Bloor Koreatown (Bathurst to Christie) holds the original cluster - BBQ houses, ssam joints, late-night anju spots. Newer openings lean toward sundubu, Korean fried chicken, and pojangmacha-style street food.

latin.intro: Catch-all for multi-country Latin American kitchens. The country-specific pages - Mexican, Peruvian, Colombian, Venezuelan, Dominican - cover most of the scene; this bucket holds spots that genuinely don't commit to one national tradition.

lebanese.intro: Shawarma, manakeesh, mezze. Toronto's Lebanese scene runs from corner shawarma counters to family-run rooms doing kibbe and warak enab. The community concentrates in North York and Mississauga.

mexican.intro: Long underrepresented in Toronto, only recently catching up. Look for the distinctions: birria places, taquerias serving real al pastor on a trompo, vs the chain Tex-Mex that dominated the 2000s. The west end clusters the newer wave.

middle_east.intro: Multi-tradition spots that don't fit cleanly into Lebanese, Turkish, Persian, or Egyptian - Mediterranean grills, generic kebab houses, mall-style shawarma counters. The country-specific pages capture the more committed kitchens.

nepalese.intro: Momos, dal bhat, sel roti. A small scene clustered in Parkdale (where Nepalese and Tibetan kitchens often share a block) and increasingly in Etobicoke.

nigerian.intro: Jollof, egusi, suya, pounded yam. The community grew quickly in the 2000s and the restaurant scene has caught up - mostly concentrated along Jane-Finch and Eglinton West.

pakistani.intro: Often shares a kitchen with Indian, but there's a distinct character - more grilled meats (boti, seekh), Mughlai-leaning curries, and Pakistani-Punjabi rather than Punjabi-Indian inflection. Brampton is the regional anchor; Scarborough has the densest Toronto-proper presence.

persian.intro: North York holds one of the largest Persian diasporas in North America, and the food shows it: kabab koobideh, ghormeh sabzi, fesenjoon, tahdig. Yonge between Steeles and Finch is the densest stretch.

peruvian.intro: Ceviche, lomo saltado, anticuchos. The scene has grown noticeably in the last five years - most spots are first-generation owned and lean coastal-Lima rather than highland.

polish.intro: Roncesvalles is the historic Polish street and the deli/pierogi counters there still anchor the scene. Newer openings have pushed into Etobicoke and Mississauga.

portuguese.intro: Little Portugal (Dundas West, College West) is the historic cluster - bifana counters, churrasqueiras, pastel de nata bakeries. The community has been in Toronto since the 1950s and the food shows it.

senegalese.intro: Thieboudienne, yassa, mafé. A small scene anchored downtown - a handful of West African spots run by Senegalese chefs, often shared with broader West African menus.

south_asian.intro: Catch-all for kitchens spanning Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Sri Lankan, or Nepalese without committing to one. Where a place leans heavily into one country's tradition, we tag it on that page instead.

spanish.intro: Tapas bars, paella spots, pintxos counters. Smaller than the Portuguese scene that often shares the same streets - newer Spanish openings in Toronto lean Basque-influenced.

sri_lankan.intro: Kothu roti, hoppers, lamprais. The community concentrates in Scarborough and the food does too - most kitchens are first-generation owned and don't compromise the spice levels.

tamil.intro: Scarborough holds one of the largest Tamil diasporas outside South Asia. Idli, dosa, biryani, and the sour-tamarind kuzhambu curries that won't show up on a generic 'Indian' menu - most Tamil spots announce themselves clearly.

thai.intro: From the long-running pad-thai houses that opened in the 90s to newer Isan-leaning kitchens doing larb, som tum, and grilled tilapia. The scene has matured noticeably since 2020.

tibetan.intro: Parkdale (sometimes called Little Tibet) is the heart of the scene - momos, thukpa, butter tea. Toronto is said to hold the largest Tibetan community in North America.

trinidadian.intro: Doubles, roti, pelau, bake-and-shark. Distinct from Jamaican despite the shared 'Caribbean' label - Trinidadian cooking carries a heavier Indo-Caribbean influence. Spots cluster in Scarborough and west of the 427.

turkish.intro: Lahmacun, döner, pide. Toronto's Turkish scene runs from corner döner counters to small kebab houses doing iskender and köfte. Several recent openings have leaned more Anatolian than Istanbul-default.

venezuelan.intro: Arepas (flatter and crispier than the Colombian round version), cachapas, tequeños. A small but growing scene driven by post-2015 migration - mostly owner-operated, mostly in the west end.

vietnamese.intro: Pho counters along Spadina opened in the 80s; the newer wave is along Bloor East where banh mi, bun bo Hue, and com tam spots have pushed past the pho-default. Vietnam's three regions are starting to show up on individual menus.
